Trying to Conceive

Can you get pregnant before, during or just after a period?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Sex during or just after a period can lead to pregnancy if it overlaps with an early fertile window. Timing varies, so knowing your usual cycle is useful but is not a guarantee against pregnancy.

Start with the fertile window, not a supposedly safe date

Pregnancy from intercourse depends on sperm being present when an egg can be fertilised. The fertile window is commonly described as the five days before ovulation and the day of ovulation. Sperm may survive for several days in favourable conditions, while an egg remains available for roughly 12 to 24 hours after release. Sex and fertilisation therefore do not have to happen on the same day.

This does not mean that fertilisation is biologically equally possible on every day of a cycle. It means that the date of ovulation is often uncertain in advance. A day that looks low-risk on a calendar may still overlap with fertility, so a period date alone cannot guarantee that unprotected sex will not lead to pregnancy.

How cycle counting works

Cycle day one is the first day of the menstrual period, and the cycle continues until the day before the next period begins. In an illustrative 28-day cycle, ovulation may occur around day 14. That example is not a rule for every person or every month. Ovulation is more usefully considered in relation to the next period than as always occurring a fixed number of days after the last one.

When pregnancy has not occurred, changes in hormone levels, including progesterone, allow the uterine lining to shed. At the same time, development towards the next ovulation can already be underway. A short cycle, such as 21 days, may bring the fertile window closer to bleeding days. Bleeding duration and cycle length are separate things: a long period does not automatically postpone ovulation.

Can sex during a period lead to pregnancy?

Yes, it can. The chance depends on when ovulation happens and how long sperm survive. Sex near the end of bleeding can overlap with the fertile window in a short cycle or when ovulation occurs earlier than expected. Menstrual blood does not act as contraception or reliably wash sperm away.

For example, if sex occurred on cycle day three and ovulation happened unusually early, around day six, surviving sperm could still be present. This is an illustration of the timing mechanism, not a prediction that day-six ovulation is usual. Lighter or brown bleeding at the end of a period does not establish a safe day, and not every episode of vaginal bleeding is a true menstrual period.

What about immediately after or before a period?

The first day or two after bleeding ends is not automatically protected. Someone with a short cycle, a longer bleed or unexpectedly early ovulation may already be approaching fertility. There is no universal percentage that can be assigned without knowing the circumstances, and an app cannot remove all uncertainty about the current cycle.

If ovulation genuinely occurred well over a day ago and the next true period is about to begin, conception from new intercourse is much less likely because that egg is no longer available. The problem is proving that timing beforehand. A late ovulation, an incorrect period prediction or bleeding for another reason can change the interpretation. Do not label the week before a predicted period as guaranteed safe.

Why a familiar pattern can change

Even generally regular cycles can vary. Some cycles may have later or earlier ovulation, or no ovulation. Life stage, illness, marked weight changes, stress and disrupted routines may contribute, while conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome can make prediction harder. Breastfeeding and the transition towards menopause can also change the pattern.

Variation is not a reason to blame yourself for a stressful week or assume that every unusual cycle means infertility. Keep a record of bleeding and relevant symptoms and seek assessment if periods are persistently irregular, absent or changing substantially. A calendar based on previous months cannot establish what the ovaries are doing today.

If pregnancy is not wanted

Use a suitable contraceptive method rather than relying on bleeding days or a green day in an ordinary period app. A taught fertility-awareness method is more than calendar counting: it may combine cycle observations, cervical mucus and temperature with specific rules about when to avoid intercourse or use a barrier. It takes training and consistent use and may be unsuitable in some circumstances.

If unprotected sex has already happened, seek emergency contraception promptly instead of waiting to see whether a period arrives. Options and time limits vary; in UK guidance, levonorgestrel pills are used within 72 hours and ulipristal within 120 hours, and a copper IUD is the most effective emergency option. A clinician should assess eligibility and timing. Condoms also help reduce sexually transmitted infections, which cycle tracking does not.

If you are trying to conceive

Regular sex every two to three days through the cycle is a practical way to cover changing fertile days without identifying one exact date. If tracking is useful to you, intercourse every one to two days during the fertile window can help. Choose an approach that feels sustainable; needing to hit one perfect day can add unnecessary pressure.

Not conceiving after a few attempts at mid-cycle sex does not prove irregular ovulation. Fertility involves several factors, including sperm, the reproductive tract, age and timing. Sex during or just after a period may cover an early fertile window, but it is not a special treatment for infertility or a requirement when it is uncomfortable.

What ovulation and progesterone tests can tell you

Urine ovulation kits detect a rise in luteinising hormone, often shortly before ovulation. A positive result may help time intercourse, but it is indirect evidence rather than proof that an egg was released. Some conditions, including PCOS, and differences between products can produce confusing or misleading results. Follow the kit instructions and discuss repeated unclear patterns with a clinician.

Progesterone rises after ovulation. Some home urine tests measure its metabolite, pregnanediol glucuronide or PdG, as an aid to confirming that ovulation has occurred. They are different from LH prediction tests and are not a complete fertility assessment. A clinician may instead arrange a blood progesterone test roughly a week before the expected next period; a universal day-21 test does not fit every cycle. One value cannot reliably measure the quality of the whole luteal phase.

Temperature, cervical mucus and app records

Basal body temperature is measured after waking and before getting up, ideally in a consistent way with a suitable thermometer. Progesterone can produce a small sustained rise after ovulation. A rise of around 0.2°C over several days may be discussed in tracking methods, but illness, sleep disruption and measurement differences affect the record. It mainly gives information after the event, not reliable advance warning of every fertile day.

A slippery cervical-mucus pattern can be useful to observe, and an app can keep these observations together. However, a prediction generated from period dates is an estimate. Neither three warmer readings nor an app colour should be used as an improvised standalone contraceptive rule. If you want to use fertility awareness to prevent pregnancy, learn a validated method from a trained practitioner.

Testing for pregnancy and knowing when to seek help

Take a pregnancy test from the first day of a missed period, following the instructions. If you do not know when the next period is due, test at least 21 days after the most recent unprotected sex. A test done too early can be negative despite pregnancy. Repeat after a few days if needed and seek advice if the period remains absent or symptoms concern you.

ASRM guidance generally recommends a fertility assessment after 12 months of trying if under 35, after six months from age 35, and potentially sooner over 40. Do not wait for those thresholds if periods are absent or markedly irregular, there is a known reproductive problem, or another reason for concern. The aim is to assess both partners or all relevant fertility factors, not assume that calendar timing is the only explanation.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Fertility depends on ovulation and sperm survival, not simply whether bleeding is present.

Calendar-app predictions are estimates; contraception requires an appropriate method.

LH, progesterone and temperature records answer different questions and have limits.

How BeMama can help

Record observations without treating an app colour as a promise. Choose either a reliable contraception plan or a manageable conception routine for your current goal.

When to seek help

Seek emergency contraception promptly after unprotected sex if pregnancy is unwanted. Persistent absent periods or unusual bleeding need clinical advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Day 14 is an example, not a universal ovulation date.
  • Sex and fertilisation may happen days apart.
  • The week before a predicted period is not guaranteed safe.
  • Use the correct timing for a pregnancy test.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get pregnant from sex during my period?

Yes. If ovulation occurs early enough, sperm from intercourse during bleeding may still be present. Bleeding is not contraception.

Are the first two days after a period always safe?

No. Short cycles, longer bleeding or early ovulation can bring those days into the fertile window.

Is pregnancy equally likely on every day of the cycle?

No. Conception depends on the fertile window. The uncertainty is knowing exactly when that window occurs, not an equal biological chance every day.

Do I always ovulate on day 14?

No. It is only a common example for a 28-day cycle. Timing can vary between people and between cycles.

Does a positive LH test prove I released an egg?

No. It detects a hormone rise that often precedes ovulation, but it is indirect evidence. Some conditions and testing patterns can produce misleading results.

Is a progesterone test always done on day 21?

No. A clinician usually times a blood test about a week before the expected next period. Day 21 is not appropriate for every cycle.

Can three warmer mornings prove that unprotected sex is safe?

No. Temperature needs interpretation within a taught fertility-awareness method. A few readings alone are not a reliable contraceptive rule.

When should I take a pregnancy test?

From the first day of a missed period, or at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex if you do not know when the next period is due.

How often should we have sex when trying?

Every two to three days across the cycle is a practical option. If tracking helps, every one to two days in the fertile window can cover the likely timing.

When should we ask for fertility assessment?

Usually after 12 months if under 35 or six months from age 35, with earlier assessment over 40 or when periods are absent, markedly irregular or another concern is known.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
